{{Short description|American researcher (1923–2007)}}

'''Charles Frederick Ehret''' (March 9, 1923 – February 24, 2007)<ref>[https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/chicagotribune/obituary.aspx?n=charles-f-ehret&pid=86642753  Dr. Charles F. Ehret]</ref> was a World War II veteran and [[molecular biologist]] who worked at Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) in [[Lemont, Illinois]], for 40 years.

Ehret researched the effects of [[electromagnetic radiation]] on [[bacillus megaterium]] with Edward Lawrence (Larry) Powers, as well as the effects of time shifts on [[Paramecium|paramecia]], rats and humans.  A graduate of City College of New York and the University of Notre Dame, Ehret formulated the term "circadian dyschronism", popularized the term ''[[zeitgeber]]'' ("time giver") in the 1980s while appearing on morning TV news shows, and helped travellers with the Jet Lag Diet,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wikihow.com/Prevent-Jet-Lag-with-a-Modified-Diet |title=How to Prevent Jet Lag with a Modified Diet: 4 Steps |website=www.wikihow.com |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170611072817/http://www.wikihow.com/Prevent-Jet-Lag-with-a-Modified-Diet |archive-date=11 June 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2007-03-03|title=Charles Ehret, 83; researcher known for developing a diet to fight jet lag|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2007-mar-03-me-ehret3-story.html|access-date=2020-12-29|website=Los Angeles Times|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Brody|first=Jane E.|date=1983-05-22|title=The Jet-Lag Diet|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/05/22/travel/the-jet-lag-diet.html|access-date=2020-12-29|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and ''The Cure for Jet Lag'' by Lynne W. Scanlon and Ehret.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Tribune|first=Joan Giangrasse Kates, Special to the|title=Dr. Charles F. Ehret: 1923 - 2007|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-2007-03-02-0703020294-story.html|access-date=2020-12-29|website=chicagotribune.com|language=en-US}}</ref>

Ehret once created the world's largest [[spectrograph]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|last=Sullivan|first=Patricia|date=4 March 2007|title=Charles F. Ehret; Devised Method to Fight Jet Lag|newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> a rainbow {{convert|100|ft}} long, that was large enough to bathe many [[Petri Dish|petri dishes]] of [[tetrahymena]] in each 100&nbsp;pm of the color spectrum.{{citation needed|date=April 2019}}

During [[World War II]], Ehret served with the Army's 87th Infantry Division.<ref name=":2" /> He was decorated with the [[Purple Heart]] and [[Bronze Star Medal|Bronze Star]].<ref name=":1" />

Ehret died at his home in [[Grayslake, Illinois]] on February 24, 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/Obituaries.asp?Page=APStory&Id=12617|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927201900/http://www.legacy.com/Obituaries.asp?Page=APStory&Id=12617|url-status=dead|archive-date=27 September 2007|title=Obituaries - Death Notices - Newspaper Obituaries - Online Obituaries - Newspaper Death Notices - Online Death Notices|website = [[Legacy.com]]|date=27 September 2007|access-date=9 April 2019}}</ref>
